learningObjectives.title: The Solar System: the Sun, planets, moons and other bodies
Orbits, gravity, orbital speed and satellites
Red-shift and evidence for an expanding universe
The Big Bang theory and the origin of the Universe

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Sun?
questions.explain: The Sun is a star at the centre of our Solar System, and the planets orbit it.

questions.q: How many planets are there in our Solar System?
questions.explain: The Solar System has eight planets, from Mercury out to Neptune.

questions.q: What name is given to a natural satellite that orbits a planet?
questions.explain: A moon is a natural satellite held in orbit around a planet by gravity.

questions.q: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our Solar System?
questions.explain: Our Solar System lies within the Milky Way, a galaxy made of billions of stars.

questions.q: Which bodies orbit the Sun on highly elliptical paths and are made mostly of ice and dust?
questions.explain: Comets are icy, dusty bodies that follow very elongated (elliptical) orbits around the Sun.

questions.q: What provides the force that keeps a planet moving in its orbit around the Sun?
questions.explain: The Sun's gravity acts on the planet, providing the centripetal force needed for orbit.

questions.q: For a satellite in a stable circular orbit, in which direction does the gravitational force on it act?
options: Away from the centre of the orbit
Towards the centre of the orbit
There is no resultant force on it
questions.explain: Gravity acts towards the centre, continually changing the satellite's direction to keep it in orbit.

questions.q: What is the orbital period of a geostationary satellite?
questions.explain: A geostationary satellite orbits with a 24-hour period so it stays above the same point on the equator.

questions.q: Which type of orbit is most suitable for a satellite that regularly scans the whole surface of the Earth, such as a weather satellite?
options: An orbit fixed above the equator
An elliptical orbit around the Sun
questions.explain: A low polar orbit passes over the poles while the Earth rotates beneath, so the satellite scans the whole surface.

questions.q: How does the orbital speed of a satellite change if it moves to an orbit with a smaller radius?
questions.explain: Satellites in lower orbits (smaller radius) must travel faster to remain in a stable orbit.

questions.q: Which equation gives the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit?
options: orbital speed = (2 x pi x orbital radius) / time period
orbital speed = time period / (2 x pi x orbital radius)
orbital speed = orbital radius x time period
orbital speed = (2 x pi x time period) / orbital radius
questions.explain: In one period the satellite travels the circumference 2 x pi x r, so speed = 2 x pi x r divided by the period.

questions.q: A satellite orbits at a radius of 1.0 x 10^7 m with an orbital period of 1.0 x 10^4 s. What is its orbital speed?
A satellite has an orbital radius of 6.0 x 10^6 m and an orbital speed of 3000 m/s. What is its orbital period?
questions.explain: Rearranging gives T = (2 x pi x 6.0 x 10^6) / 3000 = about 12 600 s.

questions.q: A moon orbits a planet at a radius of 4.0 x 10^8 m with a period of 2.4 x 10^6 s. What is its orbital speed?
Light from distant galaxies is observed to be shifted towards which part of the spectrum?
questions.explain: The light is red-shifted, meaning its wavelength is increased towards the red end of the spectrum.

questions.q: What does the red-shift of light from a distant galaxy tell us about its motion?
options: It is moving away from us
It is stationary relative to us
questions.explain: Red-shift indicates the galaxy is receding, stretching the wavelength of the light it emits.

questions.q: More distant galaxies show a greater red-shift than nearer ones. What does this observation suggest?
options: The Universe is unchanging in size
questions.explain: Greater red-shift for more distant galaxies means they recede faster, which is evidence that the Universe is expanding.

questions.q: According to current estimates, about how long ago did the Big Bang occur?
questions.explain: The Big Bang is thought to have occurred about 13.8 billion years ago, marking the start of the Universe.

questions.q: The cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is important because it is...
options: evidence that supports the Big Bang theory
radiation given off by the Sun today
proof that the Universe is not expanding
questions.explain: The CMBR is radiation left over from the early Universe and is strong evidence for the Big Bang theory.

questions.q: According to the Big Bang theory, how did the Universe begin?
options: From a very small, hot, dense region that expanded
As a large, cold, unchanging cloud
From matter created steadily over time
questions.explain: The Big Bang theory states the Universe began from an extremely small, hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since.
